questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The threat a fortified wall answers
questions.learningObjective: Identify the threat a fortified wall is designed to answer
questions.stem: Your brief asks the client to justify a curtain wall that costs a third of the site budget. Which threat does that wall answer most directly?

options.text: Attack from outside, by keeping attackers off the wall walk and off the walls
The threat of fire spreading from the village up to the gatehouse roof
options.misconception: reads the wall as a fire defence

options.text: The threat of the site's own foundation failing under the weight of the keep
options.misconception: misreads the wall as a foundation

options.text: The threat of rainwater running down the slope and undermining the ditch
options.misconception: treats the wall as a drainage work

questions.explanation: A curtain wall is a barrier: its job is to make assault expensive by keeping the wall walk out of reach and the base clear of approach. Its value is set by the threat it is meant to delay.
questions.hint: Think about what an attacker needs to reach the wall walk.

questions.topic: A described curtain wall read as a firing step
questions.learningObjective: Compute the height of a wall walk below its parapet
questions.stem: The brief describes a curtain wall 9.0 metres high with a parapet 1.2 metres tall above the wall walk, and states that a defender standing on the walk can shoot over the parapet. How many metres of the wall stand above the walk itself?
questions.explanation: The wall is 9.0 metres high in total and the parapet takes the top 1.2 metres, so the walk stands 7.8 metres above the ground. That is the height a defender must be lifted to fire from.
questions.hint: Subtract the parapet height from the total height.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a water-filled moat requires
questions.learningObjective: Identify the feature that lets a moat hold standing water

stimulus.body: The site description records a broad flat depression running the length of the defended front, with a continuous channel dug along its inner edge, a timber revetment of standing posts on the inner face, and a bottom of heavy clay that the report describes as holding water well.

questions.stem: Given the description, which single feature makes a water-filled moat possible on this site?

options.text: The width of the depression, which lets the water spread before it soaks in
options.misconception: credits the width rather than the lining

options.text: The clay bottom and revetment that allow the channel to hold a standing depth
The timber posts, which keep the banks from slumping into the channel
options.misconception: credits the revetment with holding the water

options.text: The flat ground, which lets the water be drained off into the fields
options.misconception: mistakes flat ground for a drainage benefit

questions.explanation: Water standing in a ditch depends on a bottom that will not let it away and a lining that will not collapse. The clay and the revetment supply exactly those two conditions.
questions.hint: Ask what stops the water from simply soaking away.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The second work a moat denies
questions.learningObjective: Explain the two separate denials a moat creates
questions.stem: Write a short brief note explaining why a moat is said to deny two separate works, not merely one.

answer.exemplar: A moat does two things that are usually confused. It denies the approach, because the ditch is too wide and too deep to be crossed quickly under fire and turns an attacker's charges into a slow, exposed task. It also denies the ground, because the flat, wet ground in front of the wall will not take the weight of siege engines and cannot be levelled into a ramp without filling the ditch first. The first work is crossing; the second is bringing up the heavy guns.

questions.explanation: The moat blocks the approach and denies usable ground for heavy equipment. Crossing the ditch and bringing up the artillery are separate difficulties.
questions.hint: Name the two separate difficulties the moat creates.

questions.topic: The angle of a bastion face
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a bastion face is angled rather than flat
questions.stem: Your brief specifies that a bastion's faces are angled so that an attacker can never stand square to the wall. Why is the angled face preferred?

options.text: It makes the bastion appear taller when seen from the court
options.misconception: motivates the angle by appearance

options.text: It reduces the amount of masonry needed at the corners of the bastion
options.misconception: motivates the angle by economy

options.text: It lets defenders fire along the face, hitting an attacker who is exposed to that fire
It lets rainwater run off the face and away from the wall walk
options.misconception: motivates the angle by drainage

questions.explanation: An angled face lets the defender shoot along its length, so a besieger pressed against it is caught in fire that runs the length of the wall. A flat face would leave him covered by the wall above.

questions.topic: A trace of a bastioned fort read as evidence
questions.learningObjective: Compute the frontage occupied by bastion faces
questions.stem: The brief records a surviving trace of a bastioned front 180.0 metres long, with the faces of the two bastions each set at 45 degrees to the curtain. If each bastion face is 30.0 metres long, how many metres of frontage do the four bastion faces occupy?
questions.explanation: The two bastions present four faces between them, and at 30.0 metres each they occupy 4 x 30.0 = 120.0 metres of the 180.0 metre front. The remaining 60.0 metres is the curtain between the bastions.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The height advantage of a keep
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a keep's height works through gravity and distance
questions.stem: Explain to the client why the height of a keep is described as an advantage that works by gravity and distance.

answer.exemplar: Height in a keep is not a matter of prestige but of leverage. A defender on the top of a tall keep looks down on an attacker at the foot of the wall, so every shot falls onto the near side of the target and the wall itself screens the shooter. The same defender can also drop stones and boiling liquids onto the base of the wall, and the greater the height, the longer the distance an attacking force must cross in the open.

questions.explanation: Height gives the defender the angle of the shot and increases the distance the attacker must cross. The wall screens the shooter and the drop punishes the base.
questions.hint: Say what the defender sees and what falls from above.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A described curtain wall read as a firing step
questions.learningObjective: Read parapet gaps as firing positions on a wall walk

stimulus.body: The site description records a curtain wall 3.5 metres thick, with a walkway along the top, a low parapet on the outer edge 1.2 metres high, and regularly spaced gaps in the parapet directly above the wall's internal face, each aligned with a chamber below.

questions.stem: What do the gaps in the parapet, aligned with chambers below, tell the brief's author?

options.text: The gaps are drainage slots that let rainwater leave the walk
options.misconception: mislabels the gaps as drainage

options.text: The gaps are where the parapet was rebuilt after a breach
options.misconception: reads the gaps as rebuild damage

options.text: The gaps let light from the chambers below reach the wall walk
options.misconception: gives the gaps a lighting role

options.text: The gaps are firing positions set to cover the ground at the foot of the wall

questions.explanation: Gaps in a parapet are for shooting through, and aligning them with chambers below means defenders can fire from a protected position. The alignment is the evidence, not the gap itself.
questions.hint: Ask what a defender does at a gap in a parapet.

questions.topic: The second work a moat denies
questions.learningObjective: Compute the rubble volume needed to ramp a moat
questions.stem: The brief states that a moat 12.0 metres wide with an average depth of 3.0 metres must be filled with rubble to make a ramp to the wall walk. questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A castle that becomes a residence
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a fortified residence changes when its threat passes
questions.stem: Write a brief note explaining how a fortified residence changes once the threat that built it has passed.

answer.exemplar: A building designed for defence is full of walls, small openings and few comfortable rooms, because the plan answers to attack rather than to living. When the threat recedes, those same features become inconvenient: thick walls hold up light, small windows limit a view, and circulation is organised around defence. A residence that keeps the old shell but reopens the walls is therefore a visible argument that the danger has gone, and that comfort has replaced the garrison.

questions.explanation: Defensive features are arranged against attack, so they work against comfort and view. Reopening them shows that the building's purpose has changed.
questions.hint: Say which everyday comforts the defensive plan prevents.

questions.stem: Your brief specifies a bastion face angled at 45 degrees to the curtain, with the face 30.0 metres long. What is the perpendicular distance from the tip of the bastion to the line of the curtain?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A trace of a bastioned fort read as evidence
questions.learningObjective: Read an acute angle in an earthwork as the sign of a bastion

stimulus.body: The site description records, cut into the turf and the field boundary, a long straight earthwork running east to west, interrupted twice by a projecting angular trace, and a second line of bank running parallel to the first about 25 metres away. The report notes that the projecting traces are formed of two straight sides meeting at an acute angle.

questions.stem: What does the pair of straight sides meeting at an acute angle in the earthwork tell the brief's author?

options.text: The trace is a later field wall built over an older enclosure
options.misconception: reads the trace as a field wall

options.text: The trace is a quarry boundary, and the angle marks where digging stopped
options.misconception: mislabels the angle as a quarry mark

options.text: The trace is the remains of a bastion, recognised by its two angled faces
The trace is a Roman road, and the angle marks a change of direction
options.misconception: reads the trace as a road

questions.explanation: A turf earthwork survives as banks and ditches, so its plan stays legible. Two straight sides at an acute angle is the signature of a bastion, and the parallel line is the curtain it projected from.
questions.hint: Look for the plan shape that survives in the turf.

questions.explanation: Each metre of moat holds 10.0 x 2.0 = 20 square metres of water, and 0.5 metres of depth in it gives 20 x 0.5 = 10 cubic metres. That is the volume the water supply must keep up per running metre.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The second work a moat denies
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a moat denies ground as well as approach
questions.stem: Explain to the client why a moat is said to deny the ground as well as the approach.

answer.exemplar: A moat is not only an obstacle to be crossed; it is a way of removing usable ground. A siege engine needs a flat, firm place to stand, and a ditch full of mud and standing water offers neither, so the attacker must first fill the ditch or bridge it before a single shot can be fired. That is the second denial: not that the attacker cannot come, but that the heavy work of the siege cannot even be set up where it needs to be.

questions.explanation: Filling or bridging the moat is the price of bringing up heavy equipment. The ditch denies the ground, not just the route.
questions.hint: Say what a siege engine needs that the moat denies.

questions.topic: The height advantage of a keep
questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of a keep standing above a curtain wall
questions.stem: Your brief gives a keep 40.0 metres tall and a curtain wall 10.0 metres high, and states that a defender on the keep has 30.0 metres more height. What percentage of the keep's height stands above the wall?
questions.explanation: The difference in height is 40.0 - 10.0 = 30.0 metres, and 30.0 / 40.0 = 0.75, so three quarters of the keep stands above the wall. That upper quarter is where the useful downward fire is generated.
questions.hint: Divide the height difference by the keep's height.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A castle that becomes a residence
questions.learningObjective: Read a contrast between chambers as evidence of a change of use

stimulus.body: The site description records a hall whose walls are pierced by wide, regular windows with dressed stone surrounds, and notes that the chamber has a plastered ceiling carried on moulded ribs. The report contrasts this with a chamber in the same building whose openings are arrow slits and whose ceiling is plain vaulting.

questions.stem: What does the contrast between the two chambers in the description indicate?

options.text: That the hall was designed as a dining room and the other as a prison
options.misconception: assigns the chambers a specific use

options.text: That the building serves two purposes, with one range remodelled for comfort
That the plastering is a later repair over painted decoration
options.misconception: treats the finishes as repairs

options.text: That the wide windows were never glazed and the slits were for light
options.misconception: reverses the purpose of the openings

questions.explanation: Wide windows, moulded ribs and plaster speak of comfort; slits and plain vaulting belong to the fortified building. Having both in one structure shows a process of change rather than one original purpose.
questions.hint: Ask which chamber was designed for defence and which was not.

questions.explanation: The two 30.0 metre faces at right angles close on a line of 30.0 x 1.4142 = 42.43 metres, and the triangle they enclose has an area of half of 30.0 x 30.0 = 450 square metres. That triangle is the bastion's footprint.
questions.hint: Use half the product of the two perpendicular sides.

options.text: The wall and the palisade answer exactly the same threat in the same way

questions.topic: What a water-filled moat requires
questions.learningObjective: Identify the bed condition that lets a moat hold water

stimulus.body: The site description records that the moat at the north front was dug into a bed of stiff clay, that the report notes water standing in it for years despite dry summers, and that the lower reaches are lined in places with a facing of stone set on edge.

questions.stem: Which single feature in the description most directly accounts for the moat holding water?

options.text: The length of the ditch, which gives the water time to settle
options.misconception: credits the length of the ditch

options.text: The stone facing, which holds the banks of the ditch in place
options.misconception: credits the facing with holding the water

options.text: The dry summers, which reduce the amount of water lost to evaporation
options.misconception: credits the climate for the standing water

options.text: The clay bed, which is tight enough to keep a standing depth of water in the ditch

questions.explanation: Water stands in a ditch whose bed will not let it drain away, and stiff clay is such a bed. The stone facing only holds the sides, and the dry summers do not create a supply.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The angle of a bastion face
questions.learningObjective: Explain why bastion faces are angled rather than square
questions.stem: Explain to the client why the faces of a bastion are angled rather than built square to the curtain.

answer.exemplar: A face built square to the curtain would present the besieger with a flat wall that he can shelter under while he works at its base, and a defender standing on the wall above would find his shot blocked by the parapet in front of him. Angling the face means the wall's own defenders can fire along its length, so an attacker pressed against it is caught in a flanking fire that runs the length of the masonry. The angle is a firing arrangement, not a matter of style.

questions.explanation: The angled face lets the defender shoot along the wall at an attacker who has no cover. A square face would shelter the attacker from the fire above.
questions.hint: Say where the defender's shot travels on an angled face.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a keep is placed at a corner of a wall circuit
questions.stem: Your brief asks why a keep is placed at the most defensible corner of a wall circuit rather than beside the gate. Which reason is sound?

options.misconception: motivates the position by traffic

options.text: From a corner a defender can watch and fire along two stretches of wall at once
A corner keep is cheaper to build than a round one in the middle of the circuit

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A trace of a bastioned fort read as evidence
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a surviving earthwork trace evidences a bastioned design
questions.stem: Write a brief note explaining how a surviving earthwork trace can be used as evidence of a bastioned design.

answer.exemplar: A turf earthwork keeps the plan but loses the masonry, and the plan is what a bastioned fort is defined by. Where the trace shows a long straight bank, a parallel line a fixed distance off it, and a projection formed of two straight sides at an acute angle, the survey is reading the signature of a bastion and its curtain. The angles of the trace, and the relationship between the projection and the parallel line, are more diagnostic than the size of the banks.

questions.explanation: The trace preserves plan geometry, which is precisely what identifies a bastion. Angles and the relationship between the two lines are stronger evidence than bank size.
questions.hint: Say what the geometry of the trace records.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The threat a fortified wall answers
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a fortified wall answers and what it does not
questions.stem: Explain to the client what threat a fortified wall answers and what it does not answer.

answer.exemplar: A fortified wall answers a threat of deliberate assault: it makes the approach slow, visible and costly, so that an attack which was going to succeed quickly now has to be organised, equipped and endured for weeks. It does not answer a threat of siege engines, of famine, or of a determined besieger with more men than the defenders can feed, because those are problems of supply and endurance rather than of access. The wall buys time, and time is what the garrison needed.

questions.explanation: The wall answers assault by making approach slow and exposed. It buys time rather than guaranteeing victory, so supply and endurance remain the real tests.
questions.hint: Say what the wall delays and what it cannot fix.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a water-filled moat requires
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a water-filled moat requires of bed, banks and supply
questions.stem: Write a brief note explaining what a water-filled moat requires of its bed, its banks and its water supply.

answer.exemplar: A moat that holds water needs three things: a bed that will not let the water drain away, such as clay or a lining of stone or timber; banks that will not collapse into the ditch, which is what the revetment of standing posts is for; and a supply that can replace what seeps away and what is drawn off, since a moat allowed to drain becomes a ditch an attacker can fill. The obstacle and the wetness fail separately.

questions.explanation: The bed, the banks and the supply are three separate requirements. A moat that holds water but has no supply will be a dry ditch in a season.
questions.hint: Name the three things the moat depends on.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The angle of a bastion face
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a bastion's angle turns wall thickness into a firing advantage
questions.stem: Explain to the client how the angle of a bastion's faces turns the wall's own thickness into a firing advantage.

answer.exemplar: The bastion works because the wall is thick enough to carry a walk on each face, and because the two faces meet at an acute angle, a defender standing on one of them can shoot straight along it, striking an attacker who has come up to that face for shelter. A square bastion would leave the same attacker in the dead ground of the wall above him. The angle also means that the masonry at the corner is a solid mass that nothing can be dragged up against unseen.

questions.explanation: The thickness gives room for a firing walk on the angled face, and the angle lets that walk fire along the wall. A square face would leave a dead corner at its foot.
questions.hint: Say what the walk on an angled face can shoot along.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The second work a moat denies
questions.learningObjective: Explain the two denials a moat creates and what must happen first
questions.stem: Write a brief note on why a moat is said to deny two works, and what a besieger must do before the second is possible.

answer.exemplar: A moat denies the approach, because the ditch is a barrier that must be crossed in the open and under fire, slowing any charge and exposing the men making it. It also denies the heavy work, because the ground a siege engine needs is precisely the ground the moat has taken away: flat, firm and level. Before a single gun can be brought up, the ditch has to be filled, bridged or worked around, and that delay is the real value of the moat.

questions.explanation: The moat blocks the crossing and removes the ground for the heavy work. The second denial only ends when the ditch is filled or bridged.
questions.hint: Name the two things the moat holds up.
